title: Design the Article catalogue card
description: Configure the six fields of the Article entity from the lesson. For each row pick the property name (lesson convention: camelCase in TS, snake_case in DB), the MikroORM type, and the right flag (PK, unique, nullable, default 0).

widgetConfig.prompt: Lesson 2's Article catalogue card. Pick name + type + flag for each row. The DB column names follow MikroORM's underscore naming strategy automatically.

modelAnswer: Article's spine in this course: bigint PK (room to grow past int's 2.1B ceiling), title varchar(200) NOT NULL, slug unique varchar, view_count int DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL, published_at timestamptz NULLABLE (drafts have no publish date), and metadata jsonb NULLABLE. The naming strategy maps camelCase TS to snake_case DB automatically — you write publishedAt, the column is published_at.

title: Fill in the Book entity definition
description: Complete the missing pieces of a real lesson-2 Book entity defined with `defineEntity`. The blanks cover the bigint PK, the varchar length cap, and the `nullable()` modifier the lesson stresses.

blanks.placeholder: DB modifier so the column is optional

modelAnswer: id: p.bigint().primary() — bigint, not integer, for headroom. title: p.string({ length: 200 }) — varchar(200), the course convention. publishedYear: p.integer().nullable() — the lesson hammers that .nullable() is the DB-side flag; the `?` in TypeScript is a separate concern.

title: Sort each statement: DB nullability or TypeScript optionality?
description: The lesson stresses that .nullable() (the database column flag) and '?' / '| null' (the TypeScript type flag) are two independent axes. Drop each statement into the axis it actually describes.

widgetConfig.prompt: Each statement is true of exactly one axis. Sort them. Remember: .nullable() controls whether the COLUMN can store NULL; '?' / '| null' controls whether application CODE must handle a missing value.

categories.label: TypeScript optionality — '?' / '| null'
categories.hint: About the in-memory type the compiler sees

items.label: Decides whether the generated DDL emits NOT NULL on the column.
Lets an INSERT omit the value and store NULL in that row.
Forces every consumer to narrow the value before using it, or face a compile error.
Tells the type system the property may be undefined / null in application code.
A column that is NULL in storage but a service always fills on load, so code never sees null — this axis can still mark it required.
Changing this flag produces a schema migration that alters the column constraint.

modelAnswer: MikroORM keeps the two axes separate so you can have a column that is NULL in storage but always present in memory (a service fills it on load), or the reverse. .nullable() drives the column constraint and shows up in migrations; '?' / '| null' drives the compiler's narrowing requirement in application code. Auto-deriving one from the other would force every consumer to handle null even when business logic guarantees presence — flooding the codebase with non-null assertions. They answer two different questions: 'can the row be missing this value?' versus 'can application code see undefined here?'
